text: 2008; 2 (1): 2. Also available at: http:// www.mhra.gov.uk/home/idcplg?IdcService=GET_FILE& dDocName=CON023077&RevisionSelectionMethod=Latest (accessed 26/08/08) Epilepsy and driving. Driving by patients with epilepsy is generally regulated1,2 and restricted to those whose sei- zures are adequately controlled. Also, antiepileptic drugs may produce CNS-related adverse effects, including dizzi- ness and drowsiness, that could impair a patient’s ability to drive a vehicle or operate machinery, particularly during the initial stages of therapy. In the UK,3 patients suffering from epilepsy may drive a motor vehicle (but not a heavy goods or public service ve- hicle) provided that they have had a seizure-free period of 1 year, or, if subject to attacks only while asleep, have es- tablished a 3-year period without awake attacks. It is rec- ommended that patients should not drive during withdraw- al of antiepileptic drugs, or for 6 months afterwards. 1. Berg AT, Engel J. Restricted driving for people with epilepsy. Neurology 1999; 52: 1306–7. 2. Ooi WW, Gutrecht JA. International regulations for automobile driving and epilepsy. J Travel Med 2000; 7: 1–4. 3. Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency. For medical practitioners: at a glance guide to the current medical standards of fitness to drive (issued February 2008). Available at: http://www.dvla.gov.uk/ media/pdf/medical/aagv1.pdf (accessed 09/06/08) Epilepsy and pregnancy. The management of epilepsy during pregnancy may present problems for both the mother and the fetus.1-9 The outcome of pregnancy in women with epilepsy is gen- erally recognised to be poorer than that in the general pop- ulation. Still-births and neonatal loss are increased, and maternal deaths are more common;5,7 there is also an in- creased incidence of preterm delivery and low birth- weight at term.6 In addition, there is a clearly increased risk of fetal malformation. The factors responsible for this poorer outcome are complex, and may include the disease itself, seizure frequency during pregnancy, and socio-eco- nomic factors, as well as the effects of antiepileptic drugs.1-3,5-7,10-12 A single generalised seizure does not usually pose clinical problems for the fetus, but both mother and fetus are at risk of serious trauma from maternal falls, and intra-uterine deaths have been reported. It is widely considered that sta- tus epilepticus is associated with significant mortality in mother and fetus.
